problems.question: Manganese has seven electrons outside its argon core. How are they arranged at the lowest energy?

options.label: 4s² 3d⁵, each 3d electron alone in its own orbital

problems.explanation: 4s fills first in the neutral atom, then 3d takes one electron per orbital: five 3d electrons fill all five orbitals singly, with no pair.

problems.question: Nickel's outer electrons are 4s² 3d⁸. Which arrangement does the Ni²⁺ ion have?
problems.explanation: Once the atom carries a charge its 3d level lies below 4s, so the two 4s electrons leave first and Ni²⁺ keeps all eight 3d electrons.

problems.question: Magnesium's first three ionization energies are 738, 1451 and 7733 kJ/mol. Which ion does magnesium form?
problems.explanation: The cost jumps more than fivefold at the third electron, which would come from the full inner shell, so magnesium loses two electrons and forms Mg²⁺.

problems.question: Scandium forms only the Sc³⁺ ion, and its outer electrons are 4s² 3d¹. Is scandium a transition metal by the definition used on this bench?

options.label: No: Sc³⁺ has no 3d electrons left
Yes: its atom has a 3d electron
Yes: it forms an ion with a charge of 3+
No: it is not in the fourth row

problems.explanation: Sc³⁺ has lost all three outer electrons, so its 3d subshell is empty. On this bench a transition metal must form an ion with a partly filled 3d subshell. Some books also count elements whose atoms have a partly filled d subshell, and by that rule scandium counts.

problems.question: What is the charge of the complex ion made of one Co³⁺ ion, four NH₃ molecules and two Cl− ions?
problems.explanation: Ammonia carries no charge, so the charge of the whole is the metal's +3 plus two −1 chloride ions: +3 − 2 = +1, [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺.

problems.question: Oxalate, C₂O₄²−, bonds to a metal ion through two oxygen atoms. How many oxalate ions fill all six places round Fe³⁺, and what is the charge of the whole?
problems.explanation: Each oxalate takes two places, so three fill six. Three ions of −2 bring +3 to +3 − 6 = −3: [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³−.

problems.question: Round an octahedron, how many different arrangements are there of five NH₃ and one Cl−?
problems.explanation: All six places of an octahedron are alike: any one can be turned into any other, so a single Cl− can sit in only one distinct place.

problems.question: Why is there no cis and trans form of a tetrahedral complex with two NH₃ and two Cl−?

options.label: Every pair of places in a tetrahedron is the same distance apart
A tetrahedron has only two places
Chloride cannot bond to a tetrahedral ion
Its ligands are all in one plane

problems.explanation: In a tetrahedron each place is 109.5° from every other place, so no pair is 'side by side' rather than 'opposite': all placements are one model turned.

problems.question: A solution of a nickel(II) complex takes out red light. What colour does the solution look?
problems.explanation: The colour seen is what is left of white light. Green sits opposite red on the colour wheel, so a solution that takes out red looks green.

problems.question: Ligand X gives a metal ion a wider gap than ligand Y. Which complex takes out light of shorter wavelength?
problems.explanation: A wider gap is matched by photons of more energy, and photons of more energy have a shorter wavelength.

worked.title: The gap from a wavelength
worked.setup: A chromium(III) complex takes out light of 575 nm. Find its gap in kJ for each mole of photons. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s and Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ /mol.

steps.say: What is the energy of one photon of 575 nm, in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J?
steps.hint: E = hc ÷ λ, with λ in metres: 575 nm is 575 × 10⁻⁹ m.

steps.say: What is the energy of a mole of these photons, in joules?
steps.hint: Multiply one photon's energy by Avogadro's number.

steps.say: What is that in kJ for each mole?
Titanium's gap is 239 kJ/mol. How does this chromium complex's gap compare?
steps.explain: 208 kJ/mol is less than 239, so the gap is narrower and the light taken out has a longer wavelength.

worked.finish: A gap is the energy of the photon it takes out: hc ÷ λ for one photon, times Avogadro's number for a mole.

problems.question: When the crystal field gap between the lower three and upper two d orbitals is wider than the pairing cost, how do six d electrons arrange themselves?

options.label: All six pair up in the lower three orbitals, leaving none unpaired (low spin).
Five spread singly across all five orbitals and the sixth pairs below (four unpaired).
Four fill the upper two orbitals first, leaving two below.
All six leave the ion, since the gap is too wide to hold them.

problems.explanation: Each electron takes the arrangement that costs less energy: when crossing the gap costs more than pairing, all six pair in the lower three orbitals.

problems.question: A manganese(II) complex with water has five unpaired d electrons, while a nickel(II) complex with water has two. How do their magnetic pulls compare?

options.label: The manganese(II) complex is pulled more strongly toward a magnet.
The nickel(II) complex is pulled more strongly toward a magnet.
Both are pulled by the same amount because both are +2 ions.
Neither is pulled because water ligands cancel unpaired electrons.

problems.explanation: Magnetic pull grows with the number of unpaired electrons, so five unpaired electrons give a stronger pull than two.

problems.question: What is the overall charge of the complex ion formed by a Co³⁺ ion, five neutral NH₃ molecules, and one Cl− ion?
problems.explanation: Co³⁺ (+3) plus five neutral NH₃ (0) and one Cl− (−1) gives an overall charge of +2.

problems.question: Both [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ and [Fe(CN)₆]³− hold Fe³⁺ (five d electrons). Why is [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ pulled harder by a magnet?

options.label: Water makes a narrower gap, leaving all five d electrons unpaired, whereas cyanide's wide gap pairs four of them.
Water adds extra electrons to iron(III), increasing the count to six.
Cyanide removes all d electrons from iron(III).

problems.explanation: High-spin Fe³⁺ with water has five unpaired electrons, while low-spin Fe³⁺ with cyanide has only one.
